config.title: Daily Temperatures

intro.title: Daily Temperatures
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that, given an array of daily temperatures, returns an array showing how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature for each day. You will learn to use a stack data structure to efficiently track temperatures and indices. The main technologies involved are arrays, loops, and conditional logic in JavaScript. This exercise will help you understand how to solve lessons by processing data in a single pass, which is a common pattern in algorithm design.
intro.usecase: The Daily Temperatures algorithm pattern appears in weather forecasting dashboards where you need to calculate how many days until a warmer temperature occurs. This is used in financial applications to determine waiting periods for stock prices to rise above current levels, or in e-commerce platforms to show customers how long until a price drop ends. Developers implement this when building features that require finding the next occurrence of a higher value in time-series data, such as monitoring systems tracking when metrics exceed thresholds or travel apps showing when temperatures become more favorable.

objectives: Implement a stack data structure to track temperature indices
Apply a monotonic decreasing stack pattern to process temperature data
Construct an algorithm that calculates days until warmer temperatures
Initialize an array to store results for each daily temperature
Manipulate stack indices while iterating through the temperature array
Configure the algorithm to handle edge cases like consecutive cold days
Update result values when a warmer day is found for previous temperatures

content.body: Have you ever wondered how many days you'd have to wait for a warmer temperature? In this lesson, we'll solve the Daily Temperatures lesson. We'll learn to use a clever technique to track temperatures and find waiting days efficiently.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply a single-pass approach to process temperature data.
• Implement a stack to remember temperatures and their indices.
• Explain why this method is more efficient than checking every pair of days.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: For temperature 73, which later day is warmer?
content.successMessage: Great! Day 2 (75) is warmer than day 1 (73).

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: For temperature 71, which later day is warmer?
content.successMessage: Well done! Day 6 (72) is warmer than day 4 (71).

content.title: One more
content.prompt: For temperature 69, which later day is warmer?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You checked days until you found 72 at day 6.

content.body: What you just did was check each temperature against future days until finding a warmer one. That's a brute force approach that works but becomes slow with many days.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When we have 10,000 daily temperatures, checking every future day for each temperature is too slow. We need a smarter method. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We can use a structure to remember temperatures we've encountered and check them efficiently. Think of it like a notebook where we write down temperatures we're waiting to find warmer days for.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use a single pass through the temperatures with a stack. The stack helps us remember temperatures that haven't found a warmer day yet.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73]:
• Day 0 (73): stack empty → push [0,73]
• Day 1 (74): 74 > 73 → pop 0, result[0]=1, push [1,74]
• Day 2 (75): 75 > 74 → pop 1, result[1]=1, push [2,75]
• Day 3 (71): 71 < 75 → push [3,71]
• Day 4 (69): 69 < 71 → push [4,69]
• Day 5 (72): 72 > 69 → pop 4, result[4]=1, 72 > 71 → pop 3, result[3]=2, push [5,72]
• Day 6 (76): 76 > 72 → pop 5, result[5]=1, 76 > 75 → pop 2, result[2]=4, push [6,76]
• Day 7 (73): 73 < 76 → push [7,73]
• Remaining in stack: no warmer days → result[6]=0, result[7]=0

content.body:
1. Create an array to store results (initialize with zeros).
2. Create an empty stack to store [index, temperature] pairs.
3. Loop through each temperature with its index.
4. While stack has items and current temperature > stack's top temperature:
   • Pop from stack, calculate days difference, store in results.
5. Push current [index, temperature] to stack.
6. After loop, any remaining in stack gets 0 (no warmer day).
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Initialize results array
steps.instruction: Create a results array with the same length as temperatures, filled with zeros.
steps.hint: Use the Array constructor or fill method.
steps.expectedOutcome: Array of zeros matching temperatures length
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created the results container.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Make sure it has the same length as temperatures.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try using temperatures.length to create an array of zeros.

steps.title: Create stack
steps.instruction: Initialize an empty array to use as a stack. We'll store pairs of [index, temperature].
steps.hint: Just create an empty array variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The stack is ready to store temperature data.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Just need an empty array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create an empty array, e.g., const stack = []

steps.title: Loop through temperatures
steps.instruction: Create a for loop to iterate through each temperature with its index.
steps.hint: Use for (let i = 0; i < temperatures.length; i++)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can process each temperature.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you can access both index and temperature.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let i = 0; i < temperatures.length; i++)

steps.title: Process warmer temperatures
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, add a while loop that pops from stack when current temperature > stack's top temperature. Calculate days difference and store in result.
steps.hint: Check stack length and compare temperatures. Use stack[stack.length-1] for top.
steps.expectedOutcome: While loop that updates results for warmer days
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're finding and recording warmer days.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress! Remember to calculate i - index for days difference.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: while (stack.length && currentTemp > stack[stack.length-1][1]) { const [index] = stack.pop(); result[index] = i - index; }

steps.title: Push current temperature
steps.instruction: After the while loop, push the current [index, temperature] pair to the stack. Finally, return the result array.
steps.hint: Push [i, currentTemp] to stack, then return result after the loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function that returns results array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the complete solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Don't forget to push to stack and return result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: stack.push([i, currentTemp]); after while loop, and return result; after for loop.

content.body: Great work! You've learned to solve Daily Temperatures using a stack to remember temperatures waiting for warmer days. Remember: we store indices and temperatures in the stack, check for warmer temperatures as we go, and calculate day differences. This single-pass approach is much faster than checking every pair!
content.title: Done
